extracted.intended_audience: general readers and television industry practitioners (writers, producers, casting professionals, and students of television production)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for creating, presenting, and classifying television pilot episodes used to sell or test a TV series. Covers pilot types, production/selection processes, casting, alternative models (test runs, 10/90, straight-to-series), and afterlives of pilots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a television pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: A television pilot is a standalone episode of a television series that is used to sell a show to a television broadcaster or other distributor; it is created as a testing ground to gauge whether a series will be successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine whether an entertaining concept can be realized and whether the expense of additional episodes is justified. A successful pilot may be used as the series premiere or as a later episode, and some pilots are never aired. Pilots can also be broadcast as standalone TV films or specials if the series is not ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot season process and selection metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual development cycle in which networks receive pitches, request scripts, and order pilots to evaluate new series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical U.S. broadcast pattern (as described): about 500 elevator pitches each summer, ~70 scripts requested each fall, and ~20 pilots ordered the following January. Pilots are then cast, produced, presented to studio/network executives and sometimes test audiences; networks typically choose about four to eight pilots to move to series and present them at upfronts in May. These counts and timing are used as informal benchmarks for what to expect during pilot season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise pilot introduces the characters and their world and is structured so it can function as the first episode of the series if not substantially changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subsequent changes (recasting, reshooting, rewriting) would confuse viewers, the pilot or portions of it are often re-shot or extensively reworked. Premise pilots are intended to establish exposition and origin material; examples show that heavy post-pickup changes can make a pilot unusable as-is for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of concept pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: A pilot that takes place chronologically further into the series run to demonstrate how a typical episode would appear and give executives a better feel for the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common for formats where demonstrating a 'normal' episode is important (e.g., game shows). Proofs of concept may be partially scripted (historically common for game shows) and have been subject to legal/regulatory constraints after quiz-show scandals. They show series tone and format rather than origin beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backdoor pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: An episode of an existing television show (or a film/miniseries) that heavily features characters intended for a potential spin-off, serving as a proof of concept while being broadcast within another program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backdoor pilots introduce characters to an established audience; they may air as episodes of the parent series and can succeed or fail independently of whether a new series is ultimately commissioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: A pilot that the network has contractually agreed to broadcast (as a special or series) or else pay substantial penalties to the producing studio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the contractual penalty, a put pilot usually guarantees that the pilot will be picked up by the network (or that the studio will be compensated). This is a production/contractual tool that affects the likelihood of broadcast and series pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsold pilot (busted pilot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A produced pilot episode that is never broadcast and is never turned into a television series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substantial portion of produced pilots never move to series; Variety estimates only a little over a quarter of American pilots proceed to series. Unsold pilots may later be repurposed (see theatrical release, anthology usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test run (short-run series) as alternative to single pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of episodes aired as a short-run series to test audience reaction and the viability of full production instead of commissioning a single pilot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common for shows intended to be stripped (airing five days a week) and for talk shows. Test runs and market tests can be used to pilot a format in select markets before committing to a national rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10/90 production model
rubrics_metrics.description: A model where a network broadcasts ten episodes of a new program without ordering a pilot first; if episodes reach a predetermined ratings level, the network orders 90 more episodes to reach 100 for syndication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reach syndication thresholds quickly; examples include several Tyler Perry and Debmar-Mercury series. The model depends on pre-set ratings targets and has had mixed success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight-to-series commissioning
rubrics_metrics.description: A commissioning model where a network orders an entire season without first viewing any produced episodes, so no episode is technically a pilot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically used when established talent is attached or the property/franchise is proven. The model has become more common with platforms like Netflix and can bypass traditional pilot-season dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reworking pilots into theatrical or video releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsold or re-edited pilots can be combined, extended, or appended to become theatrical releases, direct-to-video films, or similar products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples exist where unsold pilots were edited into motion pictures or direct-to-video releases; sometimes theatrical pilot versions differ substantially from televised versions (additional scenes, different credits, character fates changed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unsold pilots in anthology/summer programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Packaging unsold pilots into anthology series to air during summer months as a way to provide programming and recoup production costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically used in the U.S. (1950s–1980s) to fill summer schedules; many named anthology series aired unsold pilots. The practice declined as cable increased original summer programming and as network strategies changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting process and authority for pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting for pilots is highly competitive and often extensive; casting directors review many headshots and conduct multiple rounds of auditions before selections are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network executives generally have ultimate authority over casting decisions when deciding whether to purchase a pilot. Example: for Friends (1994), casting directors reviewed thousands of headshots and conducted multiple audition rounds before final network auditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation to executives, test audiences, and advertising/upfronts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots are presented to studio and network executives and sometimes to test audiences; chosen pilots are shown at networks' upfronts to potential advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback from executives and test audiences is used to gauge potential and to decide which pilots to pick up. Upfront presentations in May allow networks to sell the majority of advertising for new pilots and place chosen series on next season's schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting pilot pickup and survival odds
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks consider pilot quality, feedback, and the current and future potential of their existing series when deciding which pilots to order to series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a small fraction of pilots become long-running series; survival odds are low beyond the first season. Decisions factor in budget/expenditure justification, scheduling, advertising potential, and portfolio considerations of the network.
